1:
The book's long storm of words breaks at last into the quiet of submission, and the witnesses gather at the threshold of Job's final reply, 'Then Job answered the Lord.' The latin-fathers Gregory the Great, reaching in his vast commentary the very end of his labour, likens himself to a voyager who, having traversed a mighty ocean, now gains sight of the shore and lowers the sails of his intention, borne on more gently than before, though the impulse of the former blast still wafts him toward his station. Having heard the LORD unfold the strength and craft of Leviathan, and the power of the Creator who both mightily represses the enemy and mercifully protects the tempted, Gregory hears Job answer on two fronts at once: against the monster's huge strength he owns, 'I know that Thou canst do all things,' and against his hidden machinations, 'no thought is hid from Thee'; for the devil, though concealed from our infirmity by many frauds, cannot escape the notice of the Protector of the tempted.

The reformed John Gill meets the obvious objection, that Job had vowed to answer no more. He might mean only that he would not answer in the manner he had, complaining of God and justifying himself; besides, a man may change his mind without any imputation of falsehood; and above all, through what the Lord had since said to him he was now more convinced of his ignorance, mistakes, and sins, and had such a sight of God and of himself that he could not forbear speaking.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the great transition the verse opens. The words of Job justifying himself were ended at Job 31:40; the words of Job judging and condemning himself had begun at Job 40:4; and though his patience had not had its perfect work, his repentance for his impatience now had. He answers the Lord not by way of contradiction, having promised not so to answer again, but by way of submission, and thus, Henry says, we must all answer the calls of God, for true repentance begins in the acknowledgement of the truth, as at 2 Tim. 2:25.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, surveying the whole chapter from its opening, lays out the road it will travel: Job humbles himself and God accepts him; the three friends are censured; Job is commanded to offer sacrifice and pray for them; the LORD turns his captivity and doubles his affluence; his family is restored; and, having lived a hundred and forty years, he dies. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the frame for a chapter in which the great sufferer, brought at last to the end of his own words, hears God speak the vindication he could never wrest from his friends.
2:
Job's first confession is a creed of two clauses, God's omnipotence and God's omniscience, and the witnesses weigh each in turn. The reformed John Gill keeps the first clause plain: that God 'canst do every thing' is shown by the works of creation and their continual sustentation, the whole fabric of the world upheld by the hand that made it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse, 'Now I know that Thou canst do all things, and no plan is impracticable to Thee,' and fix on that word 'now.' Job had indeed known this before, but the knowledge has now risen upon him in a new, divinely-worked clearness such as he had never before experienced. Those strange and wondrous monsters, behemoth and leviathan, are to him a proof that God is able to put everything into operation, and that the plans by which he acts are beyond the reach of human comprehension. And from this a comfort steals in: if even what seemed most contradictory is, rightly perceived, so glorious, then his affliction too is no monstrous injustice, but a profoundly elaborated design, a well-digested and wise counsel of God.

On the second clause the wesleyan-arminian voices divide the sense into its two edges. Adam Clarke compresses it to a sentence, 'thy power is unlimited; thy wisdom infinite.' John Wesley opens 'no thought can be withholden from thee' both ways: there is no thought of ours that can be withholden from God's knowledge, not a fretful or unbelieving thought but he is witness to it; and there is no thought of his own that he can be hindered from bringing into execution, whatever difficulties seem to lie in the way, for whatever the Lord pleased, that has he done.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the sting of application Job now feels. He had once said this passionately, complaining at Job 23:13 that 'what his soul desireth, even that he doeth'; but now he says it with pleasure and satisfaction, that God's counsels shall stand, and that a God who can do everything can surely raise him out of the low condition he had so often foolishly despaired of as impossible. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job's repentance begins precisely here, in the glad acknowledgement of a power and wisdom against which it is the greatest madness to contend, and in whose thoughts of good the sufferer may now at last rest the very deliverance he had ceased to hope for.
3:
The verse opens with words the reader has heard before, for they are the LORD's own challenge from Job 38:2, 'Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?', and the witnesses divide over whose mouth now speaks them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes them as Job's echo of the rebuke: having heard the Almighty's speech and received his reproof, Job flings the question back upon himself, 'Alas, I am the man; I have uttered what I understood not; things too wonderful for me, that I knew not.' The reformed John Gill reads it the same way, supplying 'thou didst say' before the quotation, so that Job owns himself the foolish man who has done it and confesses it with sorrow, shame, and confusion; though he notes that Schultens would take the words as spoken by Job of God rather than of himself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a different construction altogether. The right way of understanding these verses, he argues, is after the manner of a dialogue, in which Job and the LORD alternately reply; the question was that with which God had joined the debate, and unless we assign it to him here also, we must regard it as quoted by Job and applied reflectively to himself, but it is far better, Ellicott judges, to hear it as a genuine exchange. So the debate is real: is the whole verse Job's penitent self-quotation, or is the challenge God's, answered by Job's confession?

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps to the reflective sense and fills in the confession's weight. 'What am I,' Job asks, 'that I should be guilty of such madness!'; and the 'therefore' looks back to the cause, that because his mind was without knowledge he had spoken foolishly and unadvisedly of things far above his reach.

Beneath the grammar lies the substance all the witnesses affirm, that Job here condemns the very thing God had first charged him with. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had put it in Job's mouth: that first word, 'Who is this that darkens counsel,' needed no more, for it reached his conscience and set his sin in order before him. He owns himself ignorant of the divine counsels, as all men are, for God's judgments are a great deep; the reason we quarrel with Providence is that we do not understand it, and 'things too wonderful for me' names exactly the presumption of a man who answered a matter before he heard it. The witnesses converge on a penitent who has ceased to arraign what he could never comprehend.
4:
If the previous verse borrowed God's challenge, this one borrows his summons, for 'I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me' repeats the very words with which the LORD had opened at Job 38:3 and Job 40:7, 'I will demand of thee, and answer thou me.' The reformed John Gill hears Job speaking now in a wholly altered key: not in the manner he had before, complaining of God and justifying himself, but in humble entreaty, confessing his sin and acknowledging the wisdom, goodness, and justice in all God's dealings with him that he had once arraigned. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it as pure submission, 'Hear and accept my humble confession; I will no more dispute the matter with thee, but beg information from thee'; the words God had uttered to Job by way of challenge, Job now returns to him by way of surrender.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott carries forward the dialogue-reading he had begun, and here it yields its finest fruit. This verse, he says, cannot fittingly be assigned to Job at all, but must, like the parallels in Job 38:3 and Job 40:7, be referred to God; and once it is God who says 'Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak,' then the confession of the next two verses comes in very grandly as Job's answer. Ellicott turns the moment into a mirror for every reader: how much of our knowledge of God is merely hearsay, and it is not till the experimental teaching of the Holy Ghost has revealed God to our consciences that we really see him with the inward eye; the confession of Job is therefore the confession of every converted man, analogous, in a far later sphere, to the confession of Paul at Gal. 1:16.

So the disagreement of the previous verse sharpens here to a point: Gill and Wesley put the whole verse in Job's mouth as the language of a suppliant who will teach no more but only learn, while Ellicott hands 'Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak' to God and lets Job speak only in the answering confession. Yet the two readings meet in their sense of the change that has come over the man. Whether he asks God to hear him or is himself bidden to hear, Job has laid down the posture of the disputant and taken up that of the learner, brought at last, as the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry said, to the prayer Elihu had taught him, 'that which I see not, teach thou me.' The proud cross-examiner has become the humble petitioner.
5:
'I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee' is the pivot of the whole confession, and the witnesses crowd around the contrast between report and sight. The reformed John Gill traces the hearing to its sources: Job had known God from his ancestors, who handed down in a traditionary way what they knew of his will and works; from the parents and tutors of his upbringing; and by both ordinary and extraordinary revelation, such as was granted to men in that age. The phrase 'hearing with the hearing of the ear,' Gill notes, denotes close attention, and Job had lately heard more of God, from the voice out of the whirlwind, than ever he had before.

The wesleyan-arminian voices make the seeing an inward illumination. Adam Clarke: 'I have now such a discovery of thee as I have never had before; I had only heard of thee by tradition or imperfect information, but now the eye of my mind clearly perceives thee, and in seeing thee, I see myself'; for the same light that discovers God's glory discovers Job's own meanness and vileness. John Wesley draws the same distinction: the knowledge Job had was grounded chiefly on the instructions of men, but is now clear and certain, immediately inspired by God's glorious apparition and the operation of his Holy Spirit; when the mind is enlightened by the Spirit, our knowledge of divine things as far exceeds what it was before as ocular demonstration exceeds common fame.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark this as the point where Job's tone of penitence is perfected. He acknowledges a divine omnipotence that acts according to a wisely-devised scheme, over against his own ignorance and feebleness; a whole world of divine wisdom and wondrous thoughts of God now lies open before him, and to these mysteries his affliction also belongs. He perceives it now to be a wise decree beneath which he adoringly bows, and yet it remains, even so, a mystery to him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the pastoral lesson. It is a great mercy to know the things of God by the instructions of his word and ministers, for faith comes by hearing; but when the understanding is enlightened by the Spirit of grace, our knowledge as far exceeds that by report as sight exceeds fame. God is pleased, Henry adds, to manifest himself most fully to his people by the rebukes of his word and providence: 'Now that I have been afflicted, now that I have been told of my faults, now my eye sees thee'; the rod and reproof give wisdom. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the eye which now sees God is the eye of a humbled and enlightened soul, and that such sight is the very seed of the self-abhorrence about to follow.
6:
'Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes' are the last words Job speaks in the book, and the witnesses probe both the depth of the self-loathing and the exact thing it mourns. The reformed John Gill, following Aben Ezra, would read the object as 'all my words,' the indecent expressions Job had uttered concerning God, which he now could not bear to think of but loathed, and himself on their account; for sin is abominable in its own nature and makes men so, loathsome to God and to every good man, especially when he sees it against the purity and holiness of God and the grace that forgives it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the confession to the whole man: compared with God's, Job's strength is weakness, his wisdom folly, his righteousness impurity, and so he is deeply distressed on account of the imaginations of his heart, the words of his tongue, and the acts of his life, rolling himself in the dust and sprinkling ashes on his head.

Here a real question divides the witnesses: of what, precisely, does Job repent? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the compass narrow, for Job is thoroughly humbled for his folly and unadvised speaking, for the workings and breakings-out of pride, passion, peevishness, and discontent, and for murmuring against God; even good people who have no gross enormities to repent of must be greatly afflicted in soul for such hasty, unadvised speeches. Clarke, and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, who had already called Job's words the confession of every converted man, let it run wider, to a self-abhorrence of the sinner simply, laid bare before God. Gill hovers between, naming both the particular words and the sinfulness they betray. The disagreement is one of scope, not of substance: whether Job abhors chiefly his rash speeches in the debate, or himself as a sinner altogether.

What none of them doubts is the character of true repentance the verse displays. Henry lays down its marks: it concerns us to be deeply humbled for the sins we are convinced of, not resting in a slight superficial displeasure; outward expressions of godly sorrow well become penitents, though without an inward change they do but mock God; and self-loathing is evermore the companion of true repentance, as at Ezek. 6:9, where they shall loathe themselves for the evils they have committed. Henry marks too the strange progress of Job's ashes, for his afflictions had first brought him to them at Job 2:8, when he sat down among the ashes, but now his sins bring him thither. The more Job sees of the glory and majesty of God, and of the vileness of sin, the more he abases and abhors himself, and it is in that self-abhorrence, not in any self-defence, that his long contention finds its peace.
7:
With Job's confession complete, the narrative resumes in prose, and to the reader's surprise the sentence falls not on the sufferer but on his comforters, 'ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.' The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes the reversal: while God was catechising Job out of the whirlwind one would have thought only Job was in the wrong, but here the definitive sentence is given in his favour, so that we learn to judge nothing before the time. The truly righteous may have their righteousness clouded by great afflictions, by the censures of men, and by their own frailties, and yet in due time God will bring it forth as the light, as at Ps. 37:6. Henry lingers on the tenderness of the title, for God calls him 'my servant Job' four times in two verses, owning him as dear now as before his troubles; and he had spoken the thing that was right in giving a truer account of Providence than his friends, who had made prosperity the mark of the true church and affliction the proof of God's wrath, whereas Job judged God's love and hatred by what is in men, not by what is before them, as at Eccl. 9:1.

But the witnesses press further, to ask what made the friends wrong and Job right, and here they genuinely differ. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, citing Peters, roots the whole difference in the doctrine of a future state: set that aside, and the friends, who vindicated God's exact distribution of good and evil in this life, would seem to speak more worthily than Job; but take the other life into account, and Job, who held that the righteous are sometimes afflicted here without remedy yet rewarded hereafter, and the wicked prosper here but are punished hereafter, gives the true representation, while the friends' scheme, like the Stoic maxim that virtue is its own reward, saps the very proof of a life to come. John Wesley makes the difference one of degree, 'not absolutely, but comparatively,' Job's view of the indifferency of providence's dispensations toward good and bad being truer than theirs. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott shifts the ground from doctrine to spirit: the verdict rests rather on the tone and temper of what the friends said than on their actual words, many of which are conspicuous for wisdom and beauty; their fault was to think that the cause of God must be upheld at all risks, and that it might even be required to tell lies for God, as Job had charged at Job 13:7.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley note who is spared and who is named: Eliphaz is addressed as the eldest and ringleader who spoke first and led the rest, while Elihu is not reproved, having dealt more mercifully and rebuked only Job's expressions, not his person. Henry adds the sweetest note of all, that God, before Job is exalted, makes the friends' peace depend on the intercession of the very man they had condemned, so that our quarrels with God begin on our part, but the reconciliation begins on his.
8:
The remedy God prescribes is at once a sacrifice and a humiliation, for the friends must bring 'seven bullocks and seven rams' and carry them to the man they had judged. The reformed John Gill notes that these were the creatures used in sacrifice before the Levitical law, the very number Balaam offered in the country of Moab, not far from where Job lived nor long from his age; and he reads them as typical of Christ, strong creatures, especially the bullocks used for labour, the sevenfold number pointing at the perfection of that one sacrifice to which these men were directed to look for the complete atonement of their sins.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same coincidence into a dating argument: it is remarkable that the offering prescribed for Job's friends is just that which Balaam prescribed for Balak at Numbers 23:2, one indication among many that the age of Job was that of Moses or before it. And he marvels at the justice of the appointment, for 'my servant Job shall pray for you' was the very promise with which Eliphaz himself had closed his last speech, now turned back upon him in fulfilment. Job's intercession, Ellicott adds, shows his character to be a typical one, representing Christ the sufferer and mediator; and since Job bears no trace of acquaintance with the divine covenant, the book becomes a kind of anticipation of the Gospel to the Gentile world, in which God deals with men on a principle of mediation, whether the mediator be Moses, or Job outside the covenant, or Jesus Christ.

His fellow grammatical-historical witnesses Keil and Delitzsch fix on the clause 'only his person will I accept, that I recompense not unto you your folly,' and on the word rendered 'right.' Some, they note, would translate it 'sincere,' making it Job's inward truthfulness against the friends' speaking contrary to their conscience; but the Hebrew means rather 'correct,' what is straight or established, and here objective truth and subjective truthfulness are blended, the correctness in Job's speeches lying in his having refused to make suffering the certain proof of guilt.

The wesleyan-arminian voices draw the pastoral and priestly point. Adam Clarke sees in the command a full proof of Job's innocence, for as he had once offered burnt-offerings for his own children at Job 1:5, he is now made priest and intercessor for his accusers, God thus clearing his character and confounding their devices. John Wesley hears God own the man they had defamed: 'my servant, whom though you condemned as a hypocrite, I own for my faithful servant; offer by the hand of Job, whom I hereby constitute your priest, lest my just judgment take hold of you for your false and foolish speeches.' The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the friends' road back to God runs through the prayers of the brother they had wounded.
9:
The three friends do not argue or delay, for 'they went, and did according as the LORD commanded them,' and the witnesses read their prompt obedience as the measure of a true submission. The reformed John Gill notes simply that, having taken the appointed creatures for sacrifice, they went with them to Job, the men who had come to instruct him now coming to be prayed for by him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the humbling of it. They were good men, and as soon as they understood the mind of the Lord they did as he commanded, and that speedily and without gainsaying, though it went hard against flesh and blood to court the man they had condemned. Those who would be reconciled to God, Henry says, must carefully use the prescribed means of reconciliation; peace with God is to be had only in his own way and upon his own terms, and those terms will never seem hard to such as know how to value the privilege. Job's friends had all joined in accusing him, and now they join in begging his pardon, for those who have sinned together should repent together.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the theological order of the scene. Jehovah has now risen up as a witness for Job; the spiritual redemption is already accomplished, and all that remains is that the God who has acknowledged and testified to his servant should also act outwardly and visibly, and in mercy show himself the righteous One. The acceptance of Job's person is the hinge on which the outward restoration will turn.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lifts the closing clause, 'the LORD also accepted Job,' into its highest register: as Job prayed and offered sacrifice for those who had grieved and wounded his spirit, so Christ prayed and died for his persecutors, and ever lives making intercession for the transgressors. Henry had made the same turn, noting that the text does not merely say God accepted them but that he accepted Job for them, so that, as at Eph. 1:6, we are made accepted in the beloved. And Henry adds the grace of Job's own bearing: he did not insult over his friends upon the testimony God had given him, nor upbraid them with the submission they were forced to make; God being graciously reconciled to him, he was easily reconciled to them. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the congregation of the reconciled is gathered here around one accepted mediator, and that the friends' obedience is the door through which they pass from God's kindled wrath to his renewed favour.
10:
The turning-point of the whole book is fixed to a single act of grace, 'the LORD turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends,' and the witnesses will not let the timing be missed. The reformed John Gill is careful about what the captivity means: not literal captivity, for Job's person was never carried off, though his cattle were; nor the spiritual captivity of sin, from which he had been freed years before at his conversion; but his restoration from affliction and calamity to a happy state, the return of his substance, his health, and his friends, and especially his deliverance out of the hand of Satan, into which he had for a time been given.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw the moral the sentence hides in its grammar: the little word means not 'because' but 'when,' so that the moment in which Job prayed for his friends became, as the climax of a life well-pleasing to God, the very turning-point of his glory. They cite the Talmud's true proverb borrowed from this place, that he who prays for his fellow-men always finds acceptance for himself first of all.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the point the heart of the verse. Mercy did not return while Job was disputing with his friends, no, not though he had right on his side, but when he was praying for them, praying over the sacrifice he offered on their behalf; for God is better served and pleased with our warm devotions than with our warm disputations. When Job completed his repentance by this act of forgiving men their trespasses, then God completed his remission by turning his captivity. Henry sets the whole story under the apostle's words at James 5:11, 'ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord,' and reads the doubled estate as sent both to balance his losses and to recompense the confidence he had held fast, which has, as at Heb. 10:35, a great recompence of reward.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes the ancient renderings, the Vulgate's 'the Lord turned Job to repentance' and the Chaldee's 'the Word of the Lord turned the captivity,' and presses the moral edge: mercy can be shown only to the merciful, and Job, who had just cause to be irritated against his friends, must forgive them if he would be forgiven, for he who can pray for another cannot entertain enmity against him. He dismisses as unwarranted the guess that Job armed his servants and spoiled the spoilers to recover his wealth. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the intercession the completion of Job's own discipline, which was not finished till he passed from the sphere of his own sorrows to the work of praying for his friends; through that self-oblivion his deliverance was brought about, the true moral, Ellicott says, of all human history. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley closes on the cure, that all Job's bodily distempers were now thoroughly healed, probably in a moment, and his mind calmed. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the hand which had turned against Job turned his captivity the instant he turned, in prayer, toward those who had wronged him.
11:
Prosperity brings back the crowd that adversity had scattered, and 'all his brethren, and all his sisters' gather to eat bread with him and to press their gifts upon him. The reformed John Gill takes the kindred in the larger sense, all that were related to him, the same as his kinsfolk. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look on the reunion with a colder eye: prosperity now brought together those whom calamity had frightened away, for the love of men is scarcely anything but so many coarse or delicate shades of selfishness; yet Job does not thrust them back, since the judge of the final motives of human love is God, and love shown to us is more worthy of thanks than hatred.

The gifts each brought, 'every man a piece of money, and every one an earring of gold,' draw the witnesses into a question of coin and custom. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, citing Heath, finds in the scene a striking view of human friendship: the brethren who had kept their distance and the kinsfolk who had ceased to know him now condole with him on the return of his fortunes, and, by the eastern custom that none may approach a great man without a present, each brings a kesitah. That word, Clarke argues, signifies a lamb, and the versions, Vulgate, Chaldee, Septuagint, Arabic, and Syriac, all render it a lamb or sheep, so that he supposes the piece of money to have borne a lamb stamped upon it, as at Gen. 33:19; the earring of gold he takes literally as a nose-jewel.

The other grammatical-historical witness Charles Ellicott handles the same word more cautiously. The kesitah is found also in Jacob's purchase of the field at Gen. 33:19; some, comparing Abraham's purchase at Gen. 23:16, reckon its value at four shekels, though that is not certain, and tradition says only that it was a coin with the figure of a lamb stamped upon it. So the small debate stands: was the kesitah an actual lamb given in kind, as Clarke and the old versions have it, or a piece of money named from the lamb it bore, as the tradition Ellicott reports would suggest?

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sets the visit in its proper hour, when Job had humbled himself and God was reconciled to him, and reads the feasting as congratulation of God's great and glorious favour, and the bemoaning as the friends declaring the sympathy they had felt for his calamities while they lasted but had hitherto wanted opportunity to express. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, less charitable to the latecomers, calls them swallow-friends that are gone in winter and return in the spring; yet he owns that God put it into their hearts, and that their money and their earrings became, under his blessing, the small seed of a great estate. The witnesses do not divide over the mercy: the man once shunned is honoured again, and even the coin laid at his door is a token that his captivity is truly turned.
12:
The narrator now totals the mercy, 'the LORD blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning,' and lists the flocks and herds exactly doubled. The reformed John Gill hears in it the fulfilment of Bildad's own supposition, that Job's latter end should greatly increase, though Bildad had spoken it only conditionally; and he draws the lesson that sometimes the last days of a good man are his best, as David's were and Job's here, for the best wine is reserved till last. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply confirm the arithmetic, that the fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, thousand yoke of oxen, and thousand she-asses are precisely the double of the numbers at Job 1:3. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks the same exactness as a wonder of providence, extending even to so minute a matter as the tale of a man's cattle, and to the harmony by which one event answers another, for known unto God are all his works.

Charles Ellicott, another grammatical-historical voice, uses the doubling to sharpen the earlier verdict: that Job's latter end should be blessed had been the promise of all his friends, at Job 5:24 and Job 8:7 and the like, but in their mouths it was hampered with a condition that implied the falsehood of all Job's former life, and it was that unjust imputation, not the promise itself, which had offended the truth of God.

Here the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke strikes out on a line of his own, and a real difference opens. Following Heath, he asks whether the sudden increase was not the natural consequence of the friends' presents; was it not in consequence of their bringing him sheep and cattle and gold that his stock multiplied so speedily to fourteen thousand? On this reading the kinsfolk did not visit Job because he was already prosperous, but because they saw that God had turned his captivity and healed him, and so, no longer shunning him as a stricken man, joined hands with God to restore him, their gifts being under God the very cause of his renewed affluence. Against this the other witnesses let the doubling stand as the direct blessing of God, who gives us power to get wealth and who makes the little much; Gill, Wesley, and Keil and Delitzsch see in the exact doubling not a natural accumulation but a token of special favour. So the disagreement is genuine, if quiet: whether the friends' contributions were the means through which God enriched Job, as Clarke and Heath propose, or whether the increase is set down simply as the miracle of divine blessing on a man restored.

What all affirm is the theology of the total. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers it: the blessing of the LORD makes rich, and those who would thrive must keep an eye to that blessing and never sacrifice to their own net; the last works of a good man are often his best, his path shining, like the morning light, more and more unto the perfect day. The witnesses converge on a God who repays the losses he permits with an overflowing hand.
13:
When the count turns from cattle to children, an old grief is quietly healed, for Job has again 'seven sons and three daughters,' the very number the opening of the book had taken from him. The reformed John Gill observes that they are the same in number and in kind as before, and reports the guess of Nachman that they were the very same, the doubling on that view touching only his substance and his cattle, not his family. He lists the other conjectures fairly: the Targum and Jarchi read fourteen sons; some think the children doubled in their good qualities; others, that since the former children were not lost but living with God, they may now be reckoned doubled, so that the verse becomes a proof of the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body; but these senses, Gill cautions, are not to be trusted to, and whether these children were by a former wife or another is uncertain.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch embrace the very reading Gill holds at arm's length. Instead of the seven sons and three daughters he had, Job receives just the same again, and this too is a kind of doubling, since deceased children, according to the Old Testament view, are not absolutely lost, as David confessed at 2 Samuel 12:23. The author, consistent to the smallest thing, here gives us to understand that with children who die and depart from us the relation is different from that with property we have lost: the cattle are replaced twofold, but the children are restored, because the first ten are not gone but gathered. So the debate is a real and tender one, whether the equal number of children is a shortfall in the doubling, requiring the Targum's fourteen sons to make it good, or whether it is itself the truest doubling of all, the living and the departed together forming two households of the one father.

Keil and Delitzsch add a philologist's grace-note on the form of the word 'seven,' an unusual pausal shape with an old ending borrowed, they think, from the style of the primeval histories at Gen. 21:29 and Ruth 1:19, 'a septiad of sons.' They note too that the names of the sons are passed over in silence while the daughters' are designedly given, a reticence that turns the reader's eye toward the three whom the next verse will name. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the plain letter: the number is the same as before, so the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic read, though the Chaldee alone doubles the sons to fourteen. The witnesses do not divide over the comfort of it, that the last and heaviest of Job's losses, the death of all his children at once, is the loss God most gently repairs.
14:
Alone of all the children in the book, the three daughters are named, and the witnesses find in 'Jemima, and Kezia, and Keren-happuch' a small poem of Job's restored joy. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley read the first name, Jemima, as 'the day,' so the Targum takes it, given, Wesley thinks, either for her eminent beauty or because she was born in the day of Job's prosperity after his long night of affliction; though Gill notes an Arabic sense, 'a turtle' or dove, and even an Arabian country and queen of the name. Kezia both agree to be cassia, a spice of fragrant smell; and Keren-happuch Wesley glosses as 'plenty restored.'

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch turn the three names into a portrait of beauty. The first is Jemima, a dove, on account of her dove's eyes; the second Kezia, cassia, as though woven out of the odour of cinnamon; the third Keren-happuch, 'a horn of paint,' which the Septuagint Hellenized as the horn of Amalthea, not beautiful in itself but the principal cosmetic of female beauty, so that the youngest was the fairest of all, her comeliness heightened by artificial means; the three together like the three Graces, the writer keeping to the outward appearance and not disowning his Old Testament standpoint.

On the last name a genuine difference of meaning appears. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads Keren-happuch as the flowing horn, the cornucopia or horn of plenty, and records the versions' variety, the Chaldee's 'her face as splendid as the emerald,' the Vulgate's 'horn of antimony,' the Septuagint's horn of Amalthea with its fable of the goat that nursed Jupiter, and Coverdale's blunt rendering, 'Daye, Poverte, All plenteousnes.' Charles Ellicott, his fellow grammatical-historical witness, will have none of the cornucopia: Keren-happuch is the horn for containing kohl for the eyes, the paint-box with which eastern women blackened the edges of their eyelids to make the eye seem larger, as at 2 Kings 9:30 and Jer. 4:30; Kezia he ties to the cassia of Ps. 45:9, and Jemima he renders 'fair as the day.' So the witnesses divide over the youngest daughter's name, whether Keren-happuch is the horn of plenty or the horn of eye-paint, Clarke and the older versions taking the richer emblem, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch the humbler cosmetic that names a beauty rather than a fortune.

Beneath the philology all agree on the intent. The names are chosen to perpetuate the memory of God's goodness in the surprising change of Job's condition, the daybreak after darkness, the fragrance after the stench of his sores, the plenty and the beauty restored where all had been ashes. The witnesses do not divide over that: whatever the exact sense of each word, the three daughters carry their father's gratitude in their very names.
15:
'In all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job' is the narrator's tribute to the three, and the witnesses take up both their beauty and their unusual portion. The reformed John Gill reads the praise broadly, whether of the whole world or, more likely, of the country where they dwelt, and cannot forbear a spiritual turn: the people of God, the children of Christ who is Job's antitype, are all fair, without spot or wrinkle, comely through the comeliness put upon them. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks a quieter contrast, that in the Old Testament women are often praised for their beauty, but never in the New, because the beauty of holiness is brought by the gospel to a much clearer light.

The greater interest gathers around the second clause, 'their father gave them inheritance among their brethren,' for a daughter's share beside sons was no ordinary thing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear in it a note more Arabian than Israelite, since the Law of Moses grants a daughter an inheritance only where there are no sons, as at Numbers 27:8; the writer, they say, is conscious throughout that he is telling an extra-Israelite, pre-Mosaic history, and the equal division sets before us again the pleasing picture of family concord, while implying that Job's richly-dowered daughters would not have wanted suitors. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same clause the opposite way, referring it to the history of the daughters of Zelophehad at Numbers 27, who were the first allowed an inheritance among their brethren. So the witnesses divide over the custom's root: is Job's gift a window onto a patriarchal world older than the Law, where daughters might freely inherit, as Keil and Delitzsch hold, or an echo of the very Mosaic provision that first made room for such heiresses, as Clarke supposes?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, less concerned with the law than with the motive, thinks the daughters must have had some extraordinary personal merit that Job had an eye to, perhaps excelling their brethren in wisdom and piety, so that he made them co-heirs to keep them a stay and blessing to the family; he did not turn them off with small portions, as most did. The witnesses do not finally divide over the generosity of it, a father so restored that he can enrich even his daughters beyond the custom of his neighbours, and beauty and inheritance together crowning the household that grief had once emptied. Whether the writer looks back to an age before Moses or aside to the daughters of Zelophehad, the picture is the same: concord, plenty, and a father's open hand where once there had been only the wind from the wilderness and ten new graves.
16:
With the household restored, the narrator lengthens the view to the far end of Job's life, 'after this lived Job an hundred and forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons' sons, even four generations.' The reformed John Gill reckons the years from the close of his afflictions, and weighs the old opinion that if Job's age, like his goods, was doubled, he was seventy when the blow fell and lived to two hundred and ten, the common notion of the Jewish writers; more soberly, since his former children were already grown and his trial lasted, it is said, seven years, Gill judges he was fifty or sixty at the time, and probably reached about two hundred years in all, a singular blessing of God when set beside the ages of Jacob, Joseph, Moses, and Joshua.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses that how long Job had lived before his trial we cannot certainly tell. Were the Septuagint to be relied on, all would be plain, for it adds that all the years that Job lived were two hundred and forty, which would make him a hundred when his trial began; Coverdale, by contrast, read only forty years after his troubles, dropping the hundred altogether. From the figure as it stands in the Hebrew, Clarke insists, we can infer nothing about the date at which Job lived. So the witnesses differ over the sum of his days, whether a doubled span of two hundred and ten, as the Jewish reckoning would have it and Gill inclines to, or the Septuagint's two hundred and forty with a hundred years before the trial, or a total left frankly indeterminate, as Clarke prefers to leave it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch care less for the arithmetic than for the cadence, noting how the style of the primeval histories is kept to the very last words, the seeing of children and children's children to four generations echoing the close of the patriarchs' lives, as at Gen. 50:23. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry too dwells on the mercy of those four generations: though Job's children were not doubled in number, in his children's children, the crown of old men, they were more than doubled; God had ways to repair the losses and balance the griefs of a man once written childless, giving him, as he gave Adam another seed at Gen. 4:25, a posterity to comfort his age. The witnesses do not divide over the blessing itself, a life stretched out in peace, and eyes that lived to see the fourth generation of a family that had once been buried in a single day. The long years are the visible seal of the covenant faithfulness the whole chapter has been unfolding, a patriarch dying, like the fathers before him, amid a numerous and honoured seed.
17:
'So Job died, being old and full of days' is the book's last sentence, and the witnesses gather to close it with the reverence due a patriarch's grave. The reformed John Gill marks that Job died as every man must, as even Methuselah the oldest died, and as the best of men die no less than others; yet he died a good man, in the Lord, in faith and hope of eternal life and happiness, and died too in the midst of outward prosperity, with great substance and a numerous offspring about him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the close 'old, and weary of life,' and set it beside the deaths of the patriarchs, for in the very same manner Genesis records the end of Abraham and of Isaac at Gen. 25:8 and Gen. 35:29. They died satiated of life, for long life is a gift of God, but neither his greatest nor his final gift. A New Testament poet, Keil and Delitzsch reflect, would have closed the book differently, showing Job, freed from his conflict and divinely comforted, waving his palm of victory before the throne among the innumerable hosts who have washed their robes and made them white; but the Old Testament poet, who could open his book with a scene in heaven, could not so end it. Job dares in some places to believe and hope that God will acknowledge him even after death, yet this remains a purely individual aspiration of faith, the extreme of hope set against the extreme of fear.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the fullness of the life now ended. Job had seen life in all its varieties, had risen higher than all the men of the East and sunk lower in affliction than any man before him, and died only when satisfied with this life, which the Hebrew word implies; in him, Clarke says, the whole history of Providence was exemplified and many of its mysteries unfolded, so that the end of the Lord, at James 5:11, is that he is very pitiful and of tender mercy.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott closes the book as he opened it, on its great argument. This mysterious history, dealing with the deepest problems that can engage the mind, shows how the ancients met them and what help God vouchsafed apart from covenant revelation and before the dawning of the gospel; and its great lesson is the foiling of Satan's malice. The accuser had insinuated that all service of God is interested and done for advantage; Job proved that a man may love God even under the severest affliction, and the restoration that crowned him was no contradiction of that proof, since it was entirely hidden from him until long after his probation was ended, and so could have no influence on his patience and faith. Ellicott notes that Job is named but twice elsewhere in Scripture, by Ezekiel at Ezek. 14:14 and by James at James 5:11. The witnesses do not divide; they lay the patriarch in his grave old and full of days, his integrity vindicated, his losses more than repaid, and the ancient question of his book answered not by an argument but by the God who at last showed himself; and so the book of Job is ended.
